clauses.reason: The sole operative paragraph says: "do modify my order of November 17, 1933 approving the Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry by striking therefrom the conditions numbered two (2) and three (3)". It is a section 3 approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry (the modification takes effect only on that approval), so its operative effect was the code's legal force. Under section 3(b) of the Act the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor; that force was the whole operative effect of an approval. The order states no period, condition, 'until' date, stay or provisional approval of its own, and no held record cancels, suspends, modifies under section 10(b) or supersedes the code before June 14, 1935 (see earlier_end_check). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 (Pub. Res. No. 26, 74th Cong., 49 Stat. 375, approved June 14, 1935) provides: "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval on June 14, 1935. Repeal of the power to approve codes and of the provisions enforcing them removed the legal force that the approval gave the code, so this clause ended on June 14, 1935; effective date confirmed. June 16, 1935, Title I's original two-year expiry, is not an end date: section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936. A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; it is recorded as a validity characterization (an approval made under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing), not as an end date, because the decision cancelled no approving order and no held record shows this code cancelled or suspended on May 27, 1935.

EO 6620-B (1934-02-26, Franklin D. Roosevelt), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (registered grade mirror_transcription, not an original; 1465 characters). Identity: the census register lists it as 'Executive Order 6620-B—Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry, Modification of Executive Order of November 17, 1933' dated 1934-02-26; the WPA 1944 list has '1934 Feb 26 p.569: E. 0. 6438 of Nov. 17,1933,conditionallyapproving the Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry, amended to deletetwo specifiedconditions. VII NRA Codes 641.'. Page check: the mirror page record with the same source sha256 is headed 'Executive Order 6620-B—Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry, Modification of Executive Order of November 17, 1933', dated 1934-02-26, from a common-crawl capture of 2025-09-08T16:43:01Z, and its text_sha256 equals the held text's; the heading names this order's number and the date and subject agree with the text. Single operative command: the President, acting under title I, does "modify my order of November 17, 1933 approving the Code of Fair Competition for the Hotel Industry by striking therefrom the conditions numbered two (2) and three (3)". The struck conditions (as the recital describes the first of them) required further hearings within ninety days on minimum wages and a report to the President for further order; the recitals that the Administrator will review the code by June 1, 1934 and that the code had not operated long enough are findings, not commands. Under the owner's 2026-10-21 strike-and-insert ruling the amended approval continues until the parent approval ends. First end: S.J. Res. 113 section 2, June 14, 1935; no earlier end is held.

savings.reason: Acts done under the approved code before June 14, 1935, and any liability for violating it before that date, are accrued effects. The general savings statute of the time (not a held source) preserved liabilities already incurred under a repealed statute; that preservation does not keep the approval operative. Section 5 of the Act exempted from the antitrust laws "any code, agreement, or license approved, prescribed, or issued and in effect under this title" and complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days after; whatever exemption survives for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect. The proviso in section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 says the exemption "shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder" of two kinds (section 7(a) requirements, and prohibiting practices already unlawful); it names agreements, not codes, and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. No held source continues this approval after June 14, 1935 and no held source shows a prosecution continued after that date.
